# Colony History
[italic]A short history of Bosenmori Basho for new arrivals, as the Herald's archive tells it.[/italic]
## A Nitrogen World The survey rated this world honestly: stable rock, steady light, dust storms in the barrens and an atmosphere that is almost pure nitrogen. You cannot burn a fire in it and you cannot breathe it. What it could do was hold an atmosphere processor, and for the Three World Empire that was enough to grant a charter. The name came off the survey crew's charts. Nobody has agreed on what it means since.
## Shake and Bake Bosenmori Basho is what the colonial offices call a shake and bake colony. Nobody waits for the air. The processor went up first, the people came right after, and they live sealed indoors while it works on the sky. The job will take decades. Until then every door is an airlock, every shift starts with a mask check and the Filtration Department is the most important office on the payroll.
## The Settlement - The [bold]Nexus[/bold] is the heart of the colony: the main hall above, emergency operations below and a lockdown shutter on every way in. - The [bold]Administrator's Office[/bold] and the Herald's press office share a corridor west of the Nexus. It keeps both of us honest. - The [bold]Research Complex[/bold] and the [bold]Field Research Site[/bold] study what the processor is doing to the soil. - Weyland-Yutani keeps a [bold]Corporate Dome[/bold] behind shutters of its own. It does not take questions from the Herald. - The [bold]North Barrens Telecommunications Tower[/bold] is our only radio link off world.
## Law and Soldiers Colonial law is kept by constables of the Neroid Sector Policing Authority. Paratroopers of the IASF 24th Parachute Regiment train in the empty country around us, because there is nobody out there to complain about the noise.
## Pilgrim Path and the Memorial Wall The first seal failure took a work crew in the West Barrens before the colony had a clinic worth the name. Their friends carried them north, buried them under the rock and scratched their names into a wall beside the graves. The trail has been called [bold]Pilgrim Path[/bold] ever since. New arrivals walk it once, masked, to learn what the air is like on the wrong side of the glass.
The Herald started in 2171 so that every name on that wall would also be written down properly.
